math_plain: Transfer what big models learned about reasoning into a smaller model by showing it many reasoning examples and training it step-by-step.
why_math: It works because good reasoning can be decomposed into patterns. Once you show a small model which reasoning steps are correct via examples, it learns to recognize and repeat those patterns internally, getting the accuracy benefits without needing the big model at runtime.

math_plain: Identify hateful content by weighing different harmful elements (images, words, sounds) together and explaining which parts caused the decision.
why_math: It works because hate content is multimodal—harmful elements in different forms reinforce each other. By learning which elements matter and why, you separate genuine reasons for flagging from noise, and humans can verify your reasoning is sound.

math_plain: Store knowledge on separate edge devices, route queries to the best-matched device using compact summaries, and move knowledge between devices to fit their specialties.
why_math: It works because specialized knowledge bases beat generic ones under compute limits. By routing queries smartly and migrating content to well-matched devices, you get high accuracy without replicating everything everywhere or needing central coordination.

math_plain: Predict if a user will convert after clicking by fixing the mistakes that arise when training data is corrupted by noise from multiple stages.
why_math: It works because noise compounds across stages: noisy clicks plus noisy conversions create a mess. Explicitly modeling and correcting for this hierarchical noise makes loss estimates honest again, so the model learns true patterns instead of noise.

math_plain: Evaluate podcast search by testing many query versions, transcript versions, and ranking systems, then scoring results using multiple independent judges.
why_math: It works because variation hides real signal. By averaging judgments across many independent raters and testing many configurations, random disagreement cancels out and true ranking quality emerges.

math_plain: Add a memory module that stores corrections for new documents alongside an existing ranking model, freezing the model while only updating memory weights.
why_math: It works because memory is modular—new facts can be stored in a table without overwriting old patterns. By separating knowledge storage from core learning, you retain old knowledge while efficiently absorbing new documents.

why_math: It works because simulated user behavior must match real patterns to produce trustworthy rankings. Memory affects how queries change across turns; capturing the right memory model makes simulation predictions match what real users would do.

math_plain: Use a diffusion process to generate small changes to a user's history that would flip a recommendation, showing what must change for a different outcome.
why_math: It works because diffusion gradually uncovers the shape of realistic histories. By guiding the diffusion toward counterfactuals, you find minimal, semantically valid changes instead of arbitrary perturbations, making explanations actionable.

math_plain: Track how agents search multi-step by analyzing millions of real logs, measuring whether new query terms come from recently retrieved evidence.
why_math: It works because agents learn from what they retrieve. By measuring how often new terms appear in prior results, you expose whether the agent is building iteratively on evidence or diverging; this signal improves future agent design.

math_plain: Suggest the next search query by finding the most similar historical query among millions using learned nearness, weighted by session context.
why_math: It works because query patterns repeat; what humans searched before is a strong signal for what they'll search next. Learning asymmetric similarity (what query predicts what suggestion) is faster and more up-to-date than generating new queries from scratch.

math_plain: Select which knowledge source to retrieve from by learning which one the model needs most at each reasoning step, training via fine-grained rewards across steps.
why_math: It works because different experts shine at different moments. By rewarding the model for using the right expert at each step rather than just the final answer, you teach it to route intelligently; diverse experts then cover more ground.

why_math: It works because reasoning can be distilled. If you capture the reasoning steps that lead to correct verdicts and filter out wrong ones, a smaller model learns the decision rules without needing the original large model or perfect evidence.

math_plain: Iteratively retrieve evidence and reason over it to check facts, using reinforcement learning that rewards correct final verdicts and structured reasoning format.
why_math: It works because fact-checking has structure—you must gather evidence before judging. Rewarding both format compliance and correctness teaches the model to build reasoning chains that gather relevant evidence step-by-step, avoiding hallucination.
